title: The king in a busy position (part 4 of 4)
outcomes: Names the piece on a given square before using its rule, with no hint in the prompt
Taps every square the king can step to, removing squares held by its own pieces, squares next to the enemy king and squares attacked by enemy pieces
Remembers that the square behind the king on the line of a rook or bishop check is also attacked
Decides whether an enemy piece next to the king can be taken, by checking whether anything defends it, including a distant piece, a king, or a piece whose line is blocked
Ignores distant enemy pieces whose lines reach neither the king's square nor any square the king could step to or capture on

steps.text: Part 4 of 4: The king in a busy position. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**A guess of mine, [H], with no data behind it.** I suspect two slips cause most wrong king moves: forgetting a defender that stands far away, and stepping back along the line of a check. If that is right, those two questions deserve a pause before every king move. Notice which one catches you in the next items.

steps.prompt: In three sentences, explain to a friend how to find a king's legal squares. Include the square behind the king on a check line. Write it first, then read the model answer.

fields.label: Own pieces and the enemy king close squares
The square behind the king on a check line is attacked too
A piece next to the king is safe to take only if nothing defends it

steps.text: **Model answer, to compare with yours.** Name the piece first, then ask three questions of each neighbouring square: my own piece, next to the enemy king, attacked? Remember the square behind the king on a check line. A piece next to the king can be taken only when nothing defends it, however far away the defender stands, and a pinned defender still counts.

steps.prompt: In the silent items, which question did you skip first: the own piece, the enemy king, the attacked square, or the far-away defender?
